newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Jospin to raise minimum wage, push for jobs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Jospin to raise minimum wage, push for jobs.

text.p: Socialist French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin pledged on Thursday to raise the national minimum wage by four percent, offering what he said would be the biggest boost in purchasing power for the low-paid in 15 years.

"The government will propose...an increase of four percent in the SMIC (minimum wage)," Jospin told parliament in his first policy speech, provoking groans of disappointment from some of his Socialist, Communist and ecologist allies.
He added that: "Based on a rise in prices of well below one percent, this is the biggest rise in purchasing power for 15 years."

Economists said the rise was surprisingly low and was meant to send a political message that despite demands from the left wing of the Socialist-led government, rapid wage increases might have to wait until job creation grew more robust.
Communists and unions pushed for a much bigger minimum wage rise, as high as eight percent, this year.
"It's very little. This is a message to the leftists to tell them they are not in charge," said Daiwa economist Bernard Godement.

"It also indicates that in his 35-hour work week project, if something has to give, it's going to be wages. He is basically prepared to accept some loss of pay, and what he hopes is that his manoeuvre works out and boosts employment," he said.
Jospin promised to cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 without loss of pay over five years and create 700,000 youth jobs, with half in the private sector.

Jospin, swept to power in an upset election win three weeks ago, told parliament he would give "absolute priority" to creating the new jobs and promised to call a national conference on jobs, wages and working time for September.
He vowed to make employment the "raison d'etre for all government actions" and said he wanted results by the autumn.
The increase in the minimum wage will affect some two million workers who earn the current 6,406.79 francs ($1,099) a month -- equivalent to 37.91 ($6.50) an hour.
The minimum wage, which is reviewed annually, was raised by 2.5 percent in 1996. It was hiked by four percent in 1995 after President Jacques Chirac was elected.
Economists estimated that the rise would cost about five to seven billion francs but that it could be financed through spending cuts in other areas.

"It (the minimum wage rise) should be seen as reasonable and shows the strength of the prime minister vis-a-vis the Communists, said JP Morgan economist David Naude. "It sets the tone for the wages conference -- one of reasonable increases in wages."
